newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: June Irish election date seen announced Thursday.
newsitem.headline: June Irish election date seen announced Thursday.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton is expected to announce June 6 as the date for Ireland's national election on Thursday, pitting his centre-right coalition against a resurgent centre-left opposition, political sources said.
They said Bruton would formally announce the date to parliament on Thursday morning, clearing the way for an election to be held five months ahead of deadline.

Bruton's Fine Gael party and his Labour and Democratic Left coalition allies face an uphill struggle to claw back a 12 point lead the Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrat opposition parties have opened up in recent opinion polls.

The latest, published last week, showed that Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail party would poll 43 percent of votes in an election to maintain its standing as the biggest and most powerful political party in the country.
Fine Gael would win 26 percent, Labour 12 and Democratic Left two, the poll showed. This doubled a six point lead the opposition had in an opinion poll published in April.

A Fianna Fail/Progressive Democrat coalition is tipped the current favourite by Ireland's betting chain Paddy Power bookmakers who have given it odds of 11-10 with the present 'rainbow' coalition on odds of 5-4.
Bruton came to power without an election in November 1994 when the Fianna Fail-led coalition of former Prime Minister Albert Reynolds collapsed in a row over senior legal appointments.

The Labour Party, led by Foreign Minister Dick Spring, switched support to Bruton and joined forces with the leftist Democratic Left party in what has been dubbed the "rainbow coalition" of left-right interests.

Bruton's coalition is expected to campaign on the back of one of the fastest-growing economies in the European Union and a steady decline in the unemployment rate which has blighted the nation's economy for decades.

The poll will be held five months after Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn unveiled the biggest tax giveaway budget in Irish history to distribute some of the spoils of Ireland's robust economic growth over the past five years.

But Ahern, Finance Minister in the Reynolds government, is expected to to make a campaign pledge to cut the highest tax rate from 48 to 43 per cent in five years and to mount a concerted assault on long-term unemployment.
A worrying crime wave highlighted by the unsolved killing of the nation's top investigative reporter Veronica Guerin last June is also expected to figure in the campaign.

Guerin was thought to have been shot by contract killers hired by a drugs baron operating out of Ireland. Her murder shocked the country and has led to an unprecedented crackdown on the sale and use of narcotics, especially heroin.

Ahern has accused Bruton of being too soft with Britain, Ireland's partner in a slow-moving Northern Ireland peace process, and has promised to get tough with London to make sure that a negotiated settlement is hammered out.
